title: The stone that unlocked Egypt
text: The soldiers digging a fortification near the Nile delta in 1799 had no notion that they were unearthing one of archaeology's most {{1}} (FAME) objects. The slab they found — the Rosetta Stone — carries a single priestly decree in three scripts: formal hieroglyphs, everyday Demotic, and ancient Greek. Greek could be read easily; the other two could not, leaving scholars {{2}} (ABLE) to decipher them for more than a thousand years. The stone's value lies in its {{3}} (REDUNDANT): one message, three scripts — a crossword with the answers printed alongside. Decipherment still took decades, and early efforts proved {{4}} (FRUIT) because scholars insisted that every symbol depicted a whole word. The breakthrough belonged to Jean-Francois Champollion, whose {{5}} (COMBINE) of philological rigour and inspired guesswork finally cracked the code in 1822. The key was noticing that oval rings around royal names recorded their sounds phonetically, supplying the {{6}} (PRONOUNCE) of individual signs. Legend has it that he dashed from his study crying that he had it, and promptly fainted — a romantic detail his {{7}} (BIOGRAPHY) have never quite verified. The stone itself has stood in the British Museum since 1802, where calls for its return grow louder each decade — a permanent {{8}} (REMIND) that empires carry things home.

gaps.explanation: 'the most famous objects' — adjective from fame.
'leaving scholars unable to decipher' — negative prefix un-.
'lies in its redundancy' — noun from redundant.
'whose combination of rigour and guesswork' — noun from combine.
'supplying the pronunciation of signs' — noun from pronounce.
'his biographers have never verified' — the people form, plural pinned by 'have'.
